name: Ancient Art
context: It begins in ritual and the need to explain the unknown: death, gods, power. Stone, bronze and fresco are the available technology; art is inseparable from religious and funerary architecture.

artists.name: Apelles
artists.work: The most celebrated painter of antiquity (work lost)

artists.name: Timarete
artists.note: Mentioned by Pliny the Elder; one of the first women painters documented by name in Western history. None of her work survives.
artists.imgCaption: This is NOT Timarete or her work: it is a French miniature from c. 1440 (almost 1,800 years later) in which an illustrator imagined what a woman painter of antiquity might have looked like, working only from Pliny the Elder's text. The Diana she paints inside the picture is not Timarete's real work either, which is lost — it is a late Gothic interpretation. Talbot Master, Rouen. British Library, Royal 16 G V, f. 68v.

artists.name: Roman artists
artists.imgCaption: Head of a man, late Roman Republic, 1st century BCE. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Sitter and sculptor unknown — which is how most Roman portraits are catalogued.

artists.name: Iaia of Cyzicus
artists.work: Portraits and miniatures on ivory (work lost)
artists.note: According to Pliny, she painted faster and charged more than her male colleagues; she never married and worked independently. None of her work survives.
artists.imgCaption: This is not Iaia or her real work either: it is a French miniature from c. 1440 that depicts her (Boccaccio mistakenly called her "Marcia", confusing her with a Roman Vestal). It illustrates the exact anecdote Pliny tells: she painted her self-portrait with the help of a mirror, because she lived unmarried and without a model. British Library, Royal 20 C V, f. 104.

artists.name: Anonymous artists
artists.work: Ravenna mosaics — Justinian and his retinue, Basilica of San Vitale

name: Medieval Art
context: The fall of Rome leaves the Church as art's main patron. The technology is parchment, mosaic and stained glass; light filtered through coloured glass becomes a metaphor for the divine.

artists.name: Ende ("End")
artists.note: A 10th-century Spanish nun; one of the first artists identified by name in medieval European art.

artists.name: Guda
artists.note: A 12th-century German nun; she depicted herself in an illuminated initial, an unusual gesture for her time.

artists.name: Hildegard von Bingen
artists.note: Abbess, composer and visionary; her illustrated manuscripts are rarely taught as "art" despite their symbolic complexity.

name: Renaissance
context: The printing press, the rediscovery of classical texts and the rise of the Italian city-states put the human being back at the centre. Linear perspective makes it possible to depict real space for the first time.

artists.name: Sofonisba Anguissola
artists.note: Michelangelo praised her drawings, but as a woman she was barred from studying anatomy or painting nudes, and was labelled an "amateur" even though she worked as a court painter.

artists.name: Lavinia Fontana
artists.note: The first known woman to run an independent workshop and to paint female nudes, something denied to her contemporaries.

artists.name: Properzia de' Rossi
artists.work: Relief carvings in stone and bone
artists.note: The only woman sculptor included by Vasari in "The Lives", though he described her more for her personal life than for her work.

artists.name: Levina Teerlinc
artists.work: Miniatures of the court of Henry VIII

name: Baroque and Rococo
context: The Catholic Counter-Reformation and absolutist courts demand an art that moves and persuades: dramatic light, movement, theatricality. Maritime trade brings new pigments and exotic objects into painting.

artists.name: Artemisia Gentileschi
artists.note: She survived a sexual assault and a humiliating public trial; for centuries she was catalogued as her father's "pupil" instead of being recognised for her own technique and authorship.

artists.name: Judith Leyster
artists.note: Her work was sold and signed as if it were by Frans Hals until her monogram was rediscovered in the 19th century.

artists.name: Clara Peeters
artists.work: Still lifes with a self-portrait hidden in the reflections
artists.note: A pioneer of Flemish still life; she hid her own tiny reflection in goblets and jugs, almost like a signature, because she was rarely credited openly.

name: Neoclassicism and Romanticism
context: The Enlightenment and the French Revolution push a return to reason and classical civic morality; the Industrial Revolution and its human costs produce the opposite reaction: Romanticism.

artists.name: Angelica Kauffman
artists.note: One of only two women founders of London's Royal Academy in 1768; no other woman was admitted as a full member for more than 150 years.

artists.name: Caspar David Friedrich
artists.work: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog

artists.name: Constance Mayer
artists.note: She worked side by side with the painter Prud'hon for years; much of her work ended up attributed to him, and history reduced her to the category of "muse".

name: Realism and Design Reform
context: Photography frees painting from the duty to document and pushes it to show working life without idealising it. In parallel, the industrialisation of ornament creates a design crisis that Owen Jones sets out to resolve.

artists.name: Rosa Bonheur
artists.note: The best-paid woman painter in 19th-century France; she needed a special police permit to wear trousers and work in slaughterhouses and stables without being arrested.

artists.name: Elizabeth Siddal
artists.note: A Pre-Raphaelite painter and poet in her own right; history remembers her almost exclusively as the model and wife of Dante Gabriel Rossetti.

name: Impressionism and Post-Impressionism
context: Portable paint tubes and the railway make it possible to paint outdoors; colour science inspires a brushstroke that captures light in an instant. Post-Impressionism reintroduces structure and symbol.

artists.name: Berthe Morisot
artists.note: A founding member of the Impressionist group, present at its first exhibition in 1874; for decades she was described mainly as Manet's sister-in-law and model, not as a key painter of the movement.

artists.name: Mary Cassatt
artists.note: She helped introduce Impressionism to the United States and advised collectors; that role was downplayed in favour of her label as a "painter of domestic scenes".

artists.name: Marie Bracquemond
artists.note: Her husband, also a painter, felt threatened by her talent and pressured her to stop painting; she abandoned her career at the peak of her technical ability.

artists.name: Suzanne Valadon
artists.note: She posed for Renoir, Toulouse-Lautrec and Degas before it was recognised that she drew herself; it was Degas who finally promoted her own work.

name: Early Modernism
context: The automobile, electricity and cinema reshape the perception of time and space; Cubism, Fauvism and Expressionism respond by fragmenting form. It is the prelude to the First World War.

artists.name: Hilma af Klint
artists.note: She painted abstract compositions years before Kandinsky, but asked that her work not be shown until 20 years after her death because she knew the art world of her time would not take it seriously.

artists.name: Sonia Delaunay
artists.note: She co-created Orphism with her husband Robert, but for decades the movement was attributed almost exclusively to him.

artists.name: Gabriele Münter
artists.note: She kept and saved much of the group's collection during the Nazi era, but was left out of its exhibitions and official accounts because of her relationship with Kandinsky.

artists.name: Paula Modersohn-Becker
artists.note: She died at 31, weeks after giving birth; her pioneering work was almost forgotten until it was rediscovered decades later.

artists.name: Pierre Carrier-Belleuse and Auguste-François Gorguet
artists.work: Panthéon de la Guerre (1914–1918), with ~130 artists

artists.name: Daniel MacMorris
artists.work: Reconfiguration of the Panthéon for Memory Hall, Kansas City (1957–1959)

name: Interwar Avant-gardes
context: The trauma of the First World War leads Dada to declare reason itself meaningless; Surrealism, influenced by Freud, seeks the unconscious as creative territory.

artists.name: Hannah Höch
artists.note: A founding member of Berlin Dada; her male colleagues often left her out of group photos and publications of the movement she helped create.

artists.name: Sophie Taeuber-Arp
artists.note: For decades she was catalogued as "Jean Arp's wife" rather than as an independent artist, despite an extensive body of work of her own.

artists.name: Leonora Carrington
artists.note: Her family tried to have her committed to a psychiatric institution to separate her from Max Ernst; for years she was described mainly as his partner before being recognised for her own work.

artists.name: Frida Kahlo
artists.note: André Breton included her in Surrealism almost without consulting her. For years she was known more as "Diego Rivera's wife" than as a painter.

name: Post-war: Abstract Expressionism and Pop
context: New York replaces Paris as the capital of art after the Second World War. Existential anguish feeds gestural abstraction; television and advertising feed Pop Art.

artists.name: Lee Krasner
artists.note: She put much of her own career on hold to manage and promote her husband's, Jackson Pollock; her own recognition came largely after his death.

artists.name: Helen Frankenthaler
artists.note: She invented the technique of staining unprimed canvas; male artists who adopted it later received more historical credit for popularising it.

artists.name: Elaine de Kooning
artists.work: Portraitist, including an official portrait of John F. Kennedy
artists.note: A critic and painter recognised in her day; the market prioritised her husband Willem's career for decades.

artists.name: Marisol Escobar
artists.note: She was one of the most famous artists in New York in the 1960s, even more of a media figure than Warhol; she later all but vanished from the canonical accounts of Pop Art.

name: Conceptual Art, Minimalism and Performance
context: Art asks whether it still needs to be an object: the idea or the action becomes the work itself. The civil rights and feminist movements push questions of body, identity and power to the centre.

artists.name: Eva Hesse
artists.note: She died at 34; she laid foundations of post-minimalism that later artists would develop with far more institutional recognition.

artists.name: Yoko Ono
artists.note: She was a pioneer of conceptual and performance art before she met John Lennon; popular culture reduced her to the myth of "the woman who broke up the Beatles".

artists.name: Ana Mendieta
artists.note: She died in violent and controversial circumstances; for years, discussion of her work was overshadowed by the trial of her husband, the artist Carl Andre.

artists.name: Adrian Piper
artists.work: Conceptual art on race and identity

name: Contemporary, Postcolonial and Digital
context: Globalisation, the internet and artificial intelligence dissolve the idea of a single centre of art. A postcolonial critique grows, examining who was represented, who did the representing and through which visual patterns.

artists.name: Yayoi Kusama
artists.note: She worked in poverty and near-anonymity in New York in the 1960s, while male artists adopted ideas close to hers and received far more immediate recognition.

artists.name: Joiri Minaya
artists.work: Container #2 (2016), postcolonial critique of the decorative pattern
